Be bold and be yourself and seem humble and approachable. Just strike up the conversation. You may get shot down and you may make lifelong friends. If you're shot down don't worry about it and move on.

The introduction and breaking the ice is always the hardest. If it's a bar, bus, train, park, whatever where you have the opportunity to sit next to someone for an extended period, you should have the easiest route here. When you or they take a seat within a reasonable distance, a simple 'Hi, how are you?' will be successful in breaking the ice almost every time. Sometimes the conversation just strikes up there and takes off, other times you have to give a little time(one minutes or so) before you look for a tell and pry a little bit.

When I was in sales I always looked for some type of tell if the conversation didn't work. If they guy had some sort of sports team wear on that was my goto. If a girl had some sort of piercing or tattoo that was unique I'd ask if it hurt or what it meant (If you're male avoid creeping here though, touch the subject and see how she responds). All people have something their interested in and its up to you to be able to relate to it to continue the conversation.

People also like to talk about themselves. You can use this to see if they're interested and/or conceited. If they only answer short and don't ask about you then they are not interested in that conversation. If they answer in long and don't ask about you then they are most likely conceited. You can pry deeper on these people but usually they tend to be a waste of time. The person that asks about you is the one that will hold the best conversation.

Icebreaker questions/statements:

Hell it's windy today. (Smalltalk)

Tell questions/statements:

Man the Blue Jays are playing really well right now.

So what's your preferred drink here? (DONT offer to buy them one)

Once conversation is going you shouldn't need to rely on icebreakers or tell questions/statements. Go with more the where are you from? What do you do? What are your hobbies? Do you like to travel? Where have you been? Cats or dogs? Tits or ass?

It would be cool if we could direct brand new gamers to a list of popular, in-stock, fun, and diverse games that they could theoretically just put in their CSI/MM cart and purchase.

These aren't hard-and-fast rules, but let's shoot for games that:

  • are easy to teach and learn
  • play in an hour or less (after the first time, at least)
  • are consistently in-stock
  • play well with all player counts (and the wider the range, the better!)

(Feel free to suggest more/better criteria)

Let's see what I can come up with...

Hanabi - $10. SdJ winner, cooperative game for 2-5. Hits all points.
Sushi Go! - $10. Nice, simple drafting. Plays 2-5, but could possibly stretch to 6 in a pinch.
Coup - $10. Get your bluffing and deception fix. Ignoring the 2p claim, it plays 3-6.
One Night Ultimate Werewolf - $17. More, but different bluffing and deception. Plays up to ten, which is hard to beat.
Wits & Wagers - $20 and change. An absolute masterpiece of a party game. Plays 3-6, but works well with teams of 2.
Lords of Waterdeep - $35. Simple worker placement, and a good step towards more heavy-duty games. Plays well with 2-5, though you might want to ditch the mandatory quests with just two.

That's $102, which gets us free shipping!
